name: Privilege Escalation - sudo / su
description: With sudo rights or a discovered password, escalate directly. sudo -l lists what you may run; sudo su - or su - gives a root shell.

defense.why_it_works: The sudo command caches credentials for a configurable timestamp_timeout period, allowing re-use without re-entering a password. If tty_tickets is disabled, this cached authentication is valid across all terminal sessions for that user. Sudoers entries with NOPASSWD allow specified commands to run with root privileges without any password — adversaries exploit both to escalate privileges silently.
defense.prerequisites: A shell as a user with some sudo rights, or an already-cached sudo timestamp.
defense.impact: Command execution as root (or another user) — full privilege escalation wherever the sudo rules allow.
defense.detection: Correlate sudo executions (euid=0) with cases where tty_tickets is disabled or timestamp_timeout is actively abused. Detect NOPASSWD entries in /etc/sudoers followed by immediate privileged commands, or modifications to /etc/sudoers by non-root processes.
defense.artifacts: sudo invocation logs ('sudo: user : COMMAND' in /var/log/auth.log); su session entries; TTY allocation records.
defense.prevention: Ensure tty_tickets is enabled (default on macOS Sierra+) to prevent cross-terminal credential reuse. Set timestamp_timeout to 0 to require a password every time sudo is invoked. Strictly edit /etc/sudoers so that passwords are always required and users cannot spawn risky processes as higher-privilege users.
defense.evasion: sudo/su usage is normal administrative behaviour; escalating with legitimately cached or granted sudo rights blends with day-to-day admin activity rather than triggering exploit-based alerts.
defense.misconfiguration: Common introductory misconfigurations: services running as root/SYSTEM unnecessarily, default credentials unchanged, unnecessary services listening on all interfaces, lack of firewall rules exposing services externally, no monitoring or alerting on authentication failures.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Service listening on all interfaces with default creds (common in labs/staging):
ss -tlnp | grep LISTEN
# 0.0.0.0:21  (FTP on all interfaces)
# 0.0.0.0:3306 (MySQL on all interfaces — should be 127.0.0.1 only)
# 0.0.0.0:8080 (Tomcat with manager app accessible)

# Running services as root:
ps aux | grep -E '(mysql|apache|nginx|ftp)'
# root  1234  /usr/sbin/mysqld  <-- should run as 'mysql' user
defense.secure_config:
# Bind services to localhost or specific IPs (not 0.0.0.0):
# MySQL: my.cnf -> bind-address = 127.0.0.1
# Apache: Listen 127.0.0.1:80 (if behind a proxy)

# Run services as dedicated low-priv users:
# systemd unit: User=mysql Group=mysql

# Host-based firewall (ufw):
ufw default deny incoming
ufw allow from 10.10.1.0/24 to any port 22  # SSH from mgmt only
ufw allow 443  # HTTPS
ufw enable

# Change all default credentials immediately after installation
# Enable fail2ban for SSH and web services
